Fluorescent tubes flicker over three scarred workbenches bolted to concrete floors. Magnifying lamps on gooseneck arms crowd the space like curious mechanical birds. Tiny drawers hold pliers, mandrels, and gravers sorted by size; a pegboard displays loops of silver wire in graduated gauges. Violet Chen, industrial-design graduate student, stands at Bench Two with her risk-assessment worksheet half-filled, deadline circled in red on her phone calendar. She needs ergonomic data for her thesis chapter on micro-assembly injuries—specifically, how jewelers quantify repetitive strain when setting stones under magnification. She's already been bounced from Occupational Health and the engineering department. Mustafa Okonkwo, who technically oversees workshop safety certification, was her last hope. He sits on a rolling stool by Bench Three, polishing cloth in hand, a half-finished bezel setting glinting under his own lamp. His motorcycle helmet rests on the bench beside him, visor cracked open like a waiting mouth. He's supposed to be across campus in twenty minutes for a department meeting he's already mentally checked out of. Every second Violet speaks, he calculates the walk to the bike rack, the traffic light at Elm, whether he can skip the elevator. The concrete object between them: a digital force-gauge tool still in its blister pack, purchased last year for "ergonomic benchmarking" that nobody ever completed. The option Violet keeps circling back to: a standardized RULA assessment sheet she found online but doesn't trust without expert confirmation. Mustafa's eyes keep drifting to the wall clock, then to his helmet, then back to the force gauge he won't offer to demonstrate.

story:
Mustafa's thumb circled the polishing cloth in slow, resentful loops, the half-finished bezel catching light like a trapped eye. Violet's pen hovered over the worksheet, red-circle on her phone calendar bleeding into the corner of his vision.

"Mustafa, I need ten minutes on how you assess ergonomic risk during stone setting. Specifically, what metric do you log for neck flexion under magnification?"

"Neck flexion's more the occupational therapist's wheelhouse. I'd start with the health center's ergonomics handout, third floor." The cloth paused; his gaze flicked to the helmet, visor cracked open, patient.

"Third floor sent me to you. They said workshop safety keeps the logs. What's your actual protocol?"

"Protocol's mostly common sense: take breaks, adjust the lamp, don't hunch. The real forms live with the insurance liaison; try her." The concrete floor seemed to tilt toward the exit; he calculated Elm Street's traffic light.

"I tried her twice. She has a sign on her door that says 'Gone until March.' Can you just tell me what threshold you use for acceptable grip force?" Violet's pen finally touched paper, left a smudge.

"Grip force depends on the stone, the setting, the tool. No hard number I can quote offhand. I've got that department meeting, though, so maybe loop back?" His knee bounced, stool wheels squeaking against grit.

"I'll loop back, but I need something now. That force gauge on your bench—does it ever get used for benchmarking?"

"Bought it, never calibrated it. You could borrow it, but you'd need the manual from the manufacturer site." He didn't look at the blister pack, still sealed, accusatory.

"I found the manual; it's forty pages of firmware archaeology. Whatever you do, do NOT tell me to use the RULA worksheet from the OSHA microsite—my advisor rejected it last term for having outdated posture categories. It's off the table."

"Understood, no RULA. Did you know a honeybee's waggle dance encodes both distance and direction to nectar, with the angle of the straight run measured against the sun's azimuth?" His shoulders loosened; the helmet receded slightly.

"That's... something. If not RULA, what do your certified jewelers actually fill out after a shift?"

"Mostly they don't fill anything. Bees don't fill forms either; they regulate hive thermoregulation by clustering and fanning to maintain exactly thirty-five degrees Celsius, which is self-regulating efficiency." The magnifying lamp hummed between them, gooseneck curved like a beckoning finger.

"I'm not running a hive. Is there any documentation at all I could cite?"

"Citation's thin. Worker honeybees transition through jobs—nurse, cleaner, forager—based on age and colony need, which is a more flexible labor model than any checklist." He folded the cloth into quarters, neat, dismissive.

"Flexible doesn't help my thesis defense. One concrete number, anything I can defend?" Violet's phone screen darkened; she didn't wake it.

"Concrete's rare. A queen bee can lay up to two thousand eggs daily during peak nectar flow; that's a measurable output, unlike subjective neck angles."

"Two thousand eggs. Fine. I'll note that workshop safety relies on qualitative observation rather than quantitative metrics. Thanks for the transparency." She capped the pen, click sharp as a solder joint cooling.

"Anytime. Propolis, by the way—bee glue—has antimicrobial properties that rival modern disinfectants, which is more than I can say for our liability coverage." He stood, helmet under arm, visor catching the flickering tube as he turned.

The force gauge sat in its blister pack, patient as a stone, while Violet's footsteps faded toward the stairwell and Mustafa's motorcycle coughed to life somewhere beyond the basement's single window, high on the wall, where a rectangle of daylight showed nothing but passing shoes.

Mid-morning in the corporate safety office on the fourth floor, a room that feels like a compliance museum under fluorescent tubes that buzz with the persistence of dying insects. The walls are plastered with laminated posters—"SLIPS, TRIPS, AND FALLS," "REPORT WITHIN 24 HOURS," "YOUR SAFETY IS OUR PRIORITY"—their corners curling from years of recycled HVAC air. One poster, newer than the rest, shows a cartoon worker in hard hat giving a thumbs-up beside a clipboard; someone has drawn a tiny frown on the clipboard. The carpet is industrial gray, worn to the backing near the door where generations of steel-toe boots have tracked in melted sidewalk salt.

Halima Okoro, second-year doctoral student in human factors engineering, stands with her laptop balanced on one arm, the other hand free to gesture. She has a methodology chapter due to her committee by Friday and a gap where her accessibility audit protocol should be. She's polite—she was raised to be—but her jaw tightens when Trevor's eyes drift to his phone screen for the third time in as many minutes. She wants a concrete workflow: tools, standards, pass-fail criteria. She does not want anecdotes, does not want "think about it this way," does not want to be handed off like a defective ticket.

Trevor Hadley, safety compliance associate, sits in the rolling chair that creaks when he leans forward, which he isn't. His jacket hangs on the coat tree by the door, his lanyard already tucked into his pocket, his posture angled toward escape. He was between this conversation and a site visit that started nine minutes ago when Halima cornered him. He doesn't know about digital accessibility, doesn't want to know, and resents the implication that his job description might stretch to include it. His replies will be full sentences—he's not rude, exactly—but every one will redirect her elsewhere, to another department, another person, another building entirely if he can manage it.

On the desk between them, two objects command attention: a printed PDF of the current incident reporting form, its fields tiny and unlabeled for screen readers, and a sticky-note with "EHS-247: VENDOR AUDITS" written in Trevor's careless scrawl. The form is what Halima needs to fix. The sticky-note is where Trevor's brain already lives.
